newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's formal business sector exaggerated.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's formal business sector exaggerated.

text.p: Government estimates that there are at least 800,000 formal enterprises in South Africa are exaggerated by at least 20 percent, a senior government research official told legislators on Friday.
Christo Abrahams, senior research manager of the government's Ntsika enterprise promotion agency, said research for the Department of Trade and Industry could not confirm the official estimates.
"We tried to get an estimate of the number of enterprises and we found no evidence of claims that we have 800,000 formal enterprises in South Africa.
"Actually it should be lower than 600,000 and it could be far lower than 500,000 at this stage," he said.

Abrahams told the parliamentary committee on trade and industry that preliminary estimates based on VAT registrations, the October Household Survey and other sources indicated a total of 595,900 enterprises employing at least one person.
This excluded civil servants, employees of state-owned enterprises and subsistence businesses.
He told Reuters after the meeting that the figures were soft and the actual number could be considerably lower.
Abrahams said his estimate of 316,350 micro-enterprises giving work to 467,600 people probably was quite accurate.
Less firm were the estimates of 188,000 very small enterprises employing 790,400 people and 64,850 small enterprises employing 1.3 million people.
Abrahams said the estimate of 17,000 medium enterprises employing 883,100 people and 9,700 large enterprises employing 2.8 million people probably were the most accurate.
He told the committee that total employment in non-government formal business was around 6.2 million.

He said the sector estimates included 1.6 million employed in manufacturing, 1.2 million in agriculture, 836,000 in the retail and motor trades, 690,000 in mining, 535,000 in finance and business services, 489,000 in construction and 126,000 in catering and accommodation.
Abrahams was giving evidence on the revised National Small Business Bill tabled in parliament this week, which defines four classes of small business.

The bill defines micro enterprises as those employing up to five people, very small businesses as those employing up to 10 or 20 people, depending on the sector, and small businesses as those employing up to 50 people. Medium enterprises are those employing up to 100 or 200 people, depending on the sector.
The bill provides for a statutory National Small Business Development Council and for the conversion of the Ntsika agency into a statutory research arm.

Trade and Industry Department special adviser Alistair Ruiters told the committee it was too soon to estimate the cost of the development programme, which largely replaces the Small Business Development Corporation.
"For every rand that parliament votes to small business development, no more than 10 cents will be used for administration and 90 cents will get to the small business itself," he said.
